questions.question: For a positive real number a, what does the $p$-test say about the improper integral $\int_{a}^{\infty} t^{-p}\,\mathrm{d}t$?
options: It converges if and only if $p \gt 1.$
It converges if and only if $p \lt 1.$
It converges if and only if $p = 1.$
It always converges for every real p.

questions.question: For a positive real number a, what does the $p$-test say about the improper integral $\int_{0}^{a} t^{-p}\,\mathrm{d}t$?
options: It converges if and only if $p \gt 1.$
It converges if and only if $p \ge 1.$
It always diverges for every real p.
It converges if and only if $p \lt 1.$

questions.question: Use the $p$-test to classify $\displaystyle\int_0^1\frac{1}{t^2}\,\mathrm{d}t$.
options: It converges because $p=2 \gt 1$
It diverges because $p=2$ is not less than $1$
It converges because the interval is bounded
It diverges only when $p \lt 0$

questions.question: Why do $\int_a^{\infty}t^{-p}\,\mathrm{d}t$ and $\int_0^a t^{-p}\,\mathrm{d}t$ have opposite-looking conditions?
options: They test different problematic endpoints: infinity versus zero
Substituting $t=1/u$ turns one into the other with the same $p$
Near zero $t^{-p}$ stays bounded, so only the tail at infinity matters
The inequality direction depends on whether $a$ is below or above $1$

questions.question: Use the $p$-test to classify $\int_3^{\infty}t^{-1/2}\,\mathrm{d}t$.
options: It converges, because $p=\frac12<1$.
It converges, because $t^{-1/2}\to0$ as $t\to\infty$.
It converges, because the lower limit $3$ is positive.
It diverges, because $p=\frac12$ is not greater than $1$.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes the boundary case $p=1$ in the $p$-test?
options: It converges at infinity but diverges near zero.
It diverges both at infinity and near zero.
It diverges at infinity but converges near zero.
It converges both at infinity and near zero.

questions.question: Which pair of conclusions is correct for $p=\frac12$?
options: $\int_{1}^{\infty} t^{-1/2}\,\mathrm{d}t$ converges and $\int_{0}^{1} t^{-1/2}\,\mathrm{d}t$ converges.
$\int_{1}^{\infty} t^{-1/2}\,\mathrm{d}t$ converges and $\int_{0}^{1} t^{-1/2}\,\mathrm{d}t$ diverges.
$\int_{1}^{\infty} t^{-1/2}\,\mathrm{d}t$ diverges and $\int_{0}^{1} t^{-1/2}\,\mathrm{d}t$ converges.
$\int_{1}^{\infty} t^{-1/2}\,\mathrm{d}t$ diverges and $\int_{0}^{1} t^{-1/2}\,\mathrm{d}t$ diverges.

questions.question: What is the complete set of real $q$ for which $\int_1^{\infty}t^{-(q+2)}\,\mathrm{d}t$ converges?
Does the improper integral $\displaystyle\int_0^{1}\frac{1}{t^{1/2}+t^{2}}\,\mathrm{d}t$ converge, and which argument shows it?
options: It diverges: on $(0,1]$ the integrand is at most $t^{-2}$, and $\int_0^1t^{-2}\,\mathrm{d}t$ diverges.
It converges: on $(0,1]$ the integrand is at most $t^{-1/2}$, and $\int_0^1t^{-1/2}\,\mathrm{d}t$ converges.
It converges: on $(0,1]$ the integrand is at most $t^{-2}$, and the exponent $p=2$ exceeds $1$.
It diverges: the integrand is unbounded as $t\downarrow0$, so the area near $0$ is infinite.
